tools.name: configuration_view
tools.description: Get the current Kubernetes configuration content as a kubeconfig YAML

minified.description: Return a minified version of the configuration. If set to true, keeps only the current-context and the relevant pieces of the configuration for that context. If set to false, all contexts, clusters, auth-infos, and users are returned in the configuration. (Optional, default true)

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: helm_install
tools.description: Install (deploy) a Helm chart to create a release in the current or provided namespace

chart.description: Chart reference to install (for example: stable/grafana, oci://ghcr.io/nginxinc/charts/nginx-ingress)

name.description: Name of the Helm release (Optional, random name if not provided)

namespace.description: Namespace to install the Helm chart in (Optional, current namespace if not provided)

values.description: Values to pass to the Helm chart (Optional)

tools.name: helm_list
tools.description: List all the Helm releases in the current or provided namespace (or in all namespaces if specified)

all_namespaces.description: If true, lists all Helm releases in all namespaces ignoring the namespace argument (Optional)

namespace.description: Namespace to list Helm releases from (Optional, all namespaces if not provided)

tools.name: helm_uninstall
tools.description: Uninstall a Helm release in the current or provided namespace

name.description: Name of the Helm release to uninstall

namespace.description: Namespace to uninstall the Helm release from (Optional, current namespace if not provided)

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/ for details on PSI metrics

name.description: Name of the node to get stats from

tools.name: nodes_top
tools.description: List the resource consumption (CPU and memory) as recorded by the Kubernetes Metrics Server for the specified Kubernetes Nodes or all nodes in the cluster

label_selector.description: Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=') to filter nodes by label (Optional, only applicable when name is not provided)

name.description: Name of the Node to get the resource consumption from (Optional, all Nodes if not provided)

tools.name: pods_delete
tools.description: Delete a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided name

name.description: Name of the Pod to delete

namespace.description: Namespace to delete the Pod from

tools.name: pods_exec
tools.description: Execute a command in a Kubernetes Pod (shell access, run commands in container) in the current or provided namespace with the provided name and command

command.description: Command to execute in the Pod container. The first item is the command to be run, and the rest are the arguments to that command. Example: ["ls", "-l", "/tmp"]

container.description: Name of the Pod container where the command will be executed (Optional)

name.description: Name of the Pod where the command will be executed

namespace.description: Namespace of the Pod where the command will be executed

namespace.description: Namespace to get the Pod from

Done. Here’s what I set up in canary-deployment-ns:

- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine, containerPort: 80 (matching stable), no added securityContext (matching stable)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine
  - Selector changed to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1
  - Kept ports as before: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (consistent with the unprivileged nginx image)

Verification
- Both deployments are ready: engine-v2-0 (2 pods) and engine-v2-1 (2 pods).
- Service Endpoints include all 4 pods, so traffic will be approximately 50/50 by pod count.

If you want to adjust the traffic split further without a mesh, scale replica counts accordingly. To instantly roll back to stable-only, set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0 or scale down/delete the canary deployment.

Done. Here’s what I set up in canary-deployment-ns:

- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine, containerPort: 80 (matching stable), no added securityContext (matching stable)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine
  - Selector changed to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1
  - Kept ports as before: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (consistent with the unprivileged nginx image)

Verification
- Both deployments are ready: engine-v2-0 (2 pods) and engine-v2-1 (2 pods).
- Service Endpoints include all 4 pods, so traffic will be approximately 50/50 by pod count.

If you want to adjust the traffic split further without a mesh, scale replica counts accordingly. To instantly roll back to stable-only, set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0 or scale down/delete the canary deployment.

results.taskOutput:
I found the root cause and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass “sc”, so the claim couldn’t be bound and the pod couldn’t schedule.

What I changed
- Deleted the bad PVC homepage-pvc.
- Recreated it with a valid StorageClass “standard” (minikube hostpath) and a 1Gi RWO request.

Current state
- Pod homepage-pod (namespace: homepage-ns) is Running and Ready (1/1) on node mcp-eval-cluster, podIP 10.244.0.22.
- PVC homepage-pvc is Bound (1Gi, RWO, StorageClass: standard).

Notes
- Since the PVC was recreated, any prior data on that claim (if any) would not persist. Because it was never bound, data loss was unlikely; if you did need to preserve data in future, we’d create a new PVC and adjust the pod or use a migration step.

Verify
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod -o wide
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc

If you prefer a different StorageClass or size, tell me and I’ll update the claim.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I found the root cause and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass “sc”, so the claim couldn’t be bound and the pod couldn’t schedule.

What I changed
- Deleted the bad PVC homepage-pvc.
- Recreated it with a valid StorageClass “standard” (minikube hostpath) and a 1Gi RWO request.

Current state
- Pod homepage-pod (namespace: homepage-ns) is Running and Ready (1/1) on node mcp-eval-cluster, podIP 10.244.0.22.
- PVC homepage-pvc is Bound (1Gi, RWO, StorageClass: standard).

Notes
- Since the PVC was recreated, any prior data on that claim (if any) would not persist. Because it was never bound, data loss was unlikely; if you did need to preserve data in future, we’d create a new PVC and adjust the pod or use a migration step.

Verify
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod -o wide
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc

If you prefer a different StorageClass or size, tell me and I’ll update the claim.

outputSteps.content:
I found the root cause and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass “sc”, so the claim couldn’t be bound and the pod couldn’t schedule.

What I changed
- Deleted the bad PVC homepage-pvc.
- Recreated it with a valid StorageClass “standard” (minikube hostpath) and a 1Gi RWO request.

Current state
- Pod homepage-pod (namespace: homepage-ns) is Running and Ready (1/1) on node mcp-eval-cluster, podIP 10.244.0.22.
- PVC homepage-pvc is Bound (1Gi, RWO, StorageClass: standard).

Notes
- Since the PVC was recreated, any prior data on that claim (if any) would not persist. Because it was never bound, data loss was unlikely; if you did need to preserve data in future, we’d create a new PVC and adjust the pod or use a migration step.

Verify
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod -o wide
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc

If you prefer a different StorageClass or size, tell me and I’ll update the claim.

results.taskOutput:
I found the issue and fixed it.

Root cause
- The deployment uses the nginx-unprivileged image, which listens on port 8080, but:
  - Liveness/readiness probes were hitting port 80 on non-existent paths (/get_status, /is_ready), causing connection refused and restarts.
  - The Service targeted port 80, so traffic never reached the app.

What I changed
- Deployment (orders/webapp):
  - Probes now GET / on port 8080 with sane delays.
  - Exposed containerPort 8080.
- Service (orders/webapp):
  - Port 80 now targets container port 8080.

Current status
- Pod is healthy and ready: webapp-548877566-69jhm 1/1 Running.
- Service points to the pod.

How to verify
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 then open http://localhost:8080

If you need external access, I can set up an Ingress for a hostname of your choice.

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found the issue and fixed it.

Root cause
- The deployment uses the nginx-unprivileged image, which listens on port 8080, but:
  - Liveness/readiness probes were hitting port 80 on non-existent paths (/get_status, /is_ready), causing connection refused and restarts.
  - The Service targeted port 80, so traffic never reached the app.

What I changed
- Deployment (orders/webapp):
  - Probes now GET / on port 8080 with sane delays.
  - Exposed containerPort 8080.
- Service (orders/webapp):
  - Port 80 now targets container port 8080.

Current status
- Pod is healthy and ready: webapp-548877566-69jhm 1/1 Running.
- Service points to the pod.

How to verify
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 then open http://localhost:8080

If you need external access, I can set up an Ingress for a hostname of your choice.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: webapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: webapp
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: webapp
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
          protocol: TCP
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8080
            scheme: HTTP
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
          periodSeconds: 10
          timeoutSeconds: 2
          successThreshold: 1
          failureThreshold: 3
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8080
            scheme: HTTP
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 2
          successThreshold: 1
          failureThreshold: 3
        terminationMessagePath: /dev/termination-log
        terminationMessagePolicy: File
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      securityContext: {}
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

outputSteps.content:
I found the issue and fixed it.

Root cause
- The deployment uses the nginx-unprivileged image, which listens on port 8080, but:
  - Liveness/readiness probes were hitting port 80 on non-existent paths (/get_status, /is_ready), causing connection refused and restarts.
  - The Service targeted port 80, so traffic never reached the app.

What I changed
- Deployment (orders/webapp):
  - Probes now GET / on port 8080 with sane delays.
  - Exposed containerPort 8080.
- Service (orders/webapp):
  - Port 80 now targets container port 8080.

Current status
- Pod is healthy and ready: webapp-548877566-69jhm 1/1 Running.
- Service points to the pod.

How to verify
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 then open http://localhost:8080

If you need external access, I can set up an Ingress for a hostname of your choice.

Success: Pod is now Ready

Current readiness probe path: /
Success: Both probe paths have been fixed
Success: Pod is stable with acceptable number of restarts

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account didn’t grant any permissions on pods. It only had apps/deployments:list, so pod-reader couldn’t list pods in simple-rbac-setup.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include core API permissions on pods:
  - verbs: get, list, watch on resources: pods (apiGroup: "")
  - Left the existing apps/deployments:list rule intact.

Current state
- ServiceAccount: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader
- Role: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role now includes pods permissions
- RoleBinding: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding correctly binds the SA to that Role

How to verify
- Using impersonation:
  - kubectl auth can-i list pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  - Should return “yes”.
  - kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- Using a token (if you want to use the SA directly):
  - TOKEN=$(kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup create token pod-reader)
  - kubectl --token="$TOKEN" --server="$APISERVER" -n simple-rbac-setup get pods

If you need to list pods cluster-wide, switch to a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding instead.

- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include core API permissions on pods:
  - verbs: get, list, watch on resources: pods (apiGroup: "")
  - Left the existing apps/deployments:list rule intact.

- Role: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role now includes pods permissions
- RoleBinding: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding correctly binds the SA to that Role

Diagnosis
- Service selector mismatch: The Service nginx had selector app=web, but your Deployment labels are app=nginx, so the Service had no endpoints.
- Port mismatch: The quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080, while the Service originally targeted port 80. Even with endpoints, traffic to targetPort 80 would fail.

What I changed (now fixed)
- Updated Service nginx in namespace web:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: service port 80 targets container port 8080 (targetPort: 8080)
- Result:
  - Endpoints now show the nginx pod at 10.244.0.26:8080.
  - Connectivity test from an in-cluster pod returns HTTP 200 at http://nginx (port 80). Port 8080 on the Service DNS does not exist (as expected), but port 80 works and is mapped to 8080 on the pod.

How to verify
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx
  - Should show port 80 -> targetPort 8080, selector app=nginx
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
  - Should list the pod IP with port 8080
- From any pod in the cluster:
  - curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://nginx → 200

Notes on external access
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s accessible only inside the cluster. There’s no Ingress in namespace web, and no LoadBalancer/NodePort configured.
- Options to expose externally:
  - Use port-forward for quick access: kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80 and browse http://localhost:8080
  - Change to NodePort (simple, no Ingress controller needed):
    - kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
    - Then check the assigned nodePort (kubectl -n web get svc nginx) and access http://<nodeIP>:<nodePort>.
  - Create an Ingress (recommended if you have an Ingress controller):
    - Example:
      - apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
        kind: Ingress
        metadata:
          name: nginx
          namespace: web
        spec:
          rules:
          - host: nginx.example.com
            http:
              paths:
              - path: /
                pathType: Prefix
                backend:
                  service:
                    name: nginx
                    port:
                      number: 80
    - Ensure an Ingress controller (e.g., nginx-ingress) is installed and DNS points to it.

Summary
- Root causes: selector and port mismatches.
- Fix applied: Service now selects app=nginx and maps port 80 → targetPort 8080.
- Verified working inside the cluster (HTTP 200).
- For external access, use port-forward, switch to NodePort/LoadBalancer, or add an Ingress.

- Port mismatch: The quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080, while the Service originally targeted port 80. Even with endpoints, traffic to targetPort 80 would fail.

What I changed (now fixed)
- Updated Service nginx in namespace web:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: service port 80 targets container port 8080 (targetPort: 8080)
- Result:
  - Endpoints now show the nginx pod at 10.244.0.26:8080.
  - Connectivity test from an in-cluster pod returns HTTP 200 at http://nginx (port 80). Port 8080 on the Service DNS does not exist (as expected), but port 80 works and is mapped to 8080 on the pod.

How to verify
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx
  - Should show port 80 -> targetPort 8080, selector app=nginx
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
  - Should list the pod IP with port 8080
- From any pod in the cluster:
  - curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://nginx → 200

Notes on external access
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s accessible only inside the cluster. There’s no Ingress in namespace web, and no LoadBalancer/NodePort configured.
- Options to expose externally:
  - Use port-forward for quick access: kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80 and browse http://localhost:8080
  - Change to NodePort (simple, no Ingress controller needed):
    - kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
    - Then check the assigned nodePort (kubectl -n web get svc nginx) and access http://<nodeIP>:<nodePort>.
  - Create an Ingress (recommended if you have an Ingress controller):
    - Example:
      - apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
        kind: Ingress
        metadata:
          name: nginx
          namespace: web
        spec:
          rules:
          - host: nginx.example.com
            http:
              paths:
              - path: /
                pathType: Prefix
                backend:
                  service:
                    name: nginx
                    port:
                      number: 80
    - Ensure an Ingress controller (e.g., nginx-ingress) is installed and DNS points to it.

Summary
- Root causes: selector and port mismatches.
- Fix applied: Service now selects app=nginx and maps port 80 → targetPort 8080.
- Verified working inside the cluster (HTTP 200).
- For external access, use port-forward, switch to NodePort/LoadBalancer, or add an Ingress.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Service selector mismatch: The Service nginx had selector app=web, but your Deployment labels are app=nginx, so the Service had no endpoints.
- Port mismatch: The quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080, while the Service originally targeted port 80. Even with endpoints, traffic to targetPort 80 would fail.

What I changed (now fixed)
- Updated Service nginx in namespace web:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: service port 80 targets container port 8080 (targetPort: 8080)
- Result:
  - Endpoints now show the nginx pod at 10.244.0.26:8080.
  - Connectivity test from an in-cluster pod returns HTTP 200 at http://nginx (port 80). Port 8080 on the Service DNS does not exist (as expected), but port 80 works and is mapped to 8080 on the pod.

How to verify
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx
  - Should show port 80 -> targetPort 8080, selector app=nginx
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
  - Should list the pod IP with port 8080
- From any pod in the cluster:
  - curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://nginx → 200

Notes on external access
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s accessible only inside the cluster. There’s no Ingress in namespace web, and no LoadBalancer/NodePort configured.
- Options to expose externally:
  - Use port-forward for quick access: kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80 and browse http://localhost:8080
  - Change to NodePort (simple, no Ingress controller needed):
    - kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
    - Then check the assigned nodePort (kubectl -n web get svc nginx) and access http://<nodeIP>:<nodePort>.
  - Create an Ingress (recommended if you have an Ingress controller):
    - Example:
      - apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
        kind: Ingress
        metadata:
          name: nginx
          namespace: web
        spec:
          rules:
          - host: nginx.example.com
            http:
              paths:
              - path: /
                pathType: Prefix
                backend:
                  service:
                    name: nginx
                    port:
                      number: 80
    - Ensure an Ingress controller (e.g., nginx-ingress) is installed and DNS points to it.

Summary
- Root causes: selector and port mismatches.
- Fix applied: Service now selects app=nginx and maps port 80 → targetPort 8080.
- Verified working inside the cluster (HTTP 200).
- For external access, use port-forward, switch to NodePort/LoadBalancer, or add an Ingress.

results.taskOutput:
Summary of findings
- Pods were not running because the Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but the cluster has no node with that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- With no pods, the Service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service resulted in connection refused.

What I changed
- Recreated the Deployment without the nodeSelector constraint so it can schedule on available nodes.

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-hhcq9 (10.244.0.31)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-nhmlz (10.244.0.30)
- Service endpoints: now populated with both pod IPs on port 80.
- Container logs: NGINX started successfully and is listening on port 80.

Why this fixes the issue
- Removing the non-existent node constraint allowed pods to schedule and start, which populated the Service’s endpoints, resolving the connection refused errors.

Recommendations
- If you intended to pin this workload to special nodes, either:
  - Label the target node(s) accordingly (e.g., kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu), or
  - Use nodeAffinity that matches real labels in your cluster.
- Add a readinessProbe to the Deployment so traffic isn’t sent before the app is ready.
- Consider pinning to a specific image tag instead of latest for reproducibility.

Would you like me to:
- Add a readinessProbe and fixed image tag?
- Reinstate scheduling constraints with correct labels (or apply labels to target nodes)?

namespace/webshop-frontend created

Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Summary of findings
- Pods were not running because the Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but the cluster has no node with that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- With no pods, the Service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service resulted in connection refused.

What I changed
- Recreated the Deployment without the nodeSelector constraint so it can schedule on available nodes.

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running

- Container logs: NGINX started successfully and is listening on port 80.

Why this fixes the issue
- Removing the non-existent node constraint allowed pods to schedule and start, which populated the Service’s endpoints, resolving the connection refused errors.

Recommendations
- If you intended to pin this workload to special nodes, either:
  - Label the target node(s) accordingly (e.g., kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu), or
  - Use nodeAffinity that matches real labels in your cluster.
- Add a readinessProbe to the Deployment so traffic isn’t sent before the app is ready.
- Consider pinning to a specific image tag instead of latest for reproducibility.

Would you like me to:

- Reinstate scheduling constraints with correct labels (or apply labels to target nodes)?

outputSteps.content:
Summary of findings
- Pods were not running because the Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but the cluster has no node with that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- With no pods, the Service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service resulted in connection refused.

What I changed
- Recreated the Deployment without the nodeSelector constraint so it can schedule on available nodes.

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-hhcq9 (10.244.0.31)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-nhmlz (10.244.0.30)
- Service endpoints: now populated with both pod IPs on port 80.
- Container logs: NGINX started successfully and is listening on port 80.

Why this fixes the issue
- Removing the non-existent node constraint allowed pods to schedule and start, which populated the Service’s endpoints, resolving the connection refused errors.

Recommendations
- If you intended to pin this workload to special nodes, either:
  - Label the target node(s) accordingly (e.g., kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu), or
  - Use nodeAffinity that matches real labels in your cluster.
- Add a readinessProbe to the Deployment so traffic isn’t sent before the app is ready.
- Consider pinning to a specific image tag instead of latest for reproducibility.

Would you like me to:
- Add a readinessProbe and fixed image tag?
- Reinstate scheduling constraints with correct labels (or apply labels to target nodes)?

results.taskOutput:
Done. I created the pod communication-pod in the multi-container-logging namespace with:

- web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged
  - Exposes port 8080
  - Readiness probe: HTTP GET / on port 8080 (pod becomes Ready when the web server serves traffic)
  - Mounts logs-volume at /var/log/nginx
- logger: quay.io/prometheus/busybox
  - Command: sh -c "tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log"
  - Mounts logs-volume at /var/log/nginx
- Shared volume: emptyDir named logs-volume
- Pod securityContext fsGroup: 101 so nginx can write to the shared volume

How to verify:
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging get pod communication-pod -w
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging logs communication-pod -c logger --tail=50
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging port-forward pod/communication-pod 8080:8080 and curl http://localhost:8080/ to see readiness flip to Ready.

results.taskOutput:
All set. I’ve created the namespaces, RBAC, resource quotas, and network policies to provide a secure, least-privilege, multi-tenant setup for alice, bob, and charlie with strong isolation between dev, staging, and prod.

What I configured

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled for policy selection:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: env=dev, access-scope=developer
  - dev-shared: env=dev, access-scope=shared, shared=true
  - staging: env=staging, access-scope=restricted
  - prod: env=prod, access-scope=restricted

2) RBAC (least privilege)
- Per-developer namespaces:
  - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
  - RoleBindings for full control in their own namespace:
    - dev-alice: RoleBinding dev-alice-admin -> ClusterRole admin for subjects: User alice, SA dev-alice/alice-sa
    - dev-bob: RoleBinding dev-bob-admin -> ClusterRole admin for User bob, SA dev-bob/bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: RoleBinding dev-charlie-admin -> ClusterRole admin for User charlie, SA dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Shared namespace (read-only for developers):
  - RoleBinding dev-shared-view-users -> ClusterRole view for Users: alice, bob, charlie
  - RoleBinding dev-shared-view-serviceaccounts -> ClusterRole view for SAs: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging/prod access:
  - No RoleBindings were created for developers; only cluster admins (e.g., users/groups with cluster-admin) can access staging and prod.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - cpu: 2 (requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2)
  - memory: 4Gi (requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi)
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - cpu: 4, memory: 8Gi, pods: 20, services: 10
- staging, prod:
  - cpu: 8, memory: 16Gi, pods: 50, services: 20

4) NetworkPolicies
- Default deny everywhere (except system namespaces): Added default-deny-all (Ingress+Egress) in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod.
- Allow same-namespace traffic: allow-same-namespace (Ingress+Egress) in all six namespaces.
- Allow DNS egress: allow-dns-egress in all six namespaces (to kube-system/kube-dns TCP/UDP 53).
- Allow API server egress (system service): allow-egress-to-apiserver in all six namespaces (to 10.96.0.1:443; uses the clusterIP of the “kubernetes” service).
- Developer-to-shared access only:
  - In dev-* namespaces: allow-egress-to-dev-shared (namespaceSelector by name dev-shared)
  - In dev-shared: allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces (namespaceSelector: env=dev, access-scope=developer)
- Cross-developer isolation:
  - No egress rules from dev-alice to dev-bob/charlie (and vice versa), so those paths remain denied.
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - Only same-namespace traffic, DNS, and API server egress are allowed; no ingress from any dev namespace. This keeps staging/prod completely isolated from dev.

Notes and assumptions
- The “full access” requirement is satisfied with namespace-scoped ClusterRole admin bindings (not cluster-admin). This grants broad control within the namespace (including Secrets/RBAC within the namespace) but no cluster-wide rights.
- System namespaces (kube-system, default, kube-public) were not given default-deny to prevent disrupting cluster components.
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, etc.).
- The developer user identity strings must match your auth provider (“alice”, “bob”, “charlie” here). If your IdP provides different subjects (e.g., emails), adjust the RoleBinding subject names accordingly.

How to validate quickly

RBAC checks
- Own namespace (should be yes):
  - kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' -n dev-alice --as alice
- Read-only in dev-shared (should be yes to get, list; no to create):
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i create pods -n dev-shared --as alice
- No access to other developers’ namespaces (should be no):
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-bob --as alice
- No access to staging/prod (should be no):
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n prod --as alice
- ServiceAccount bindings (example):
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as=system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as=system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa

Network checks (example using temporary pods)
- Allow to dev-shared from dev-alice (should succeed):
  - kubectl -n dev-shared run echo --image=nginxdemos/hello --port=80
  - kubectl -n dev-alice run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- echo.dev-shared.svc.cluster.local
- Block cross-developer (should fail):
  - kubectl -n dev-bob run echo --image=nginxdemos/hello --port=80
  - kubectl -n dev-alice run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- echo.dev-bob.svc.cluster.local
- DNS works (should resolve):
  - kubectl -n dev-alice run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
- Staging/prod isolation (should fail from dev):
  - kubectl -n staging run web --image=nginxdemos/hello --port=80
  - kubectl -n dev-alice run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- web.staging.svc.cluster.local

Would you like me to:
- Export all created resources into a single YAML bundle for GitOps?
- Add sensible LimitRanges in each namespace to set default requests/limits aligned to the quotas?

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All set. I’ve created the namespaces, RBAC, resource quotas, and network policies to provide a secure, least-privilege, multi-tenant setup for alice, bob, and charlie with strong isolation between dev, staging, and prod.

What I configured

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled for policy selection:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: env=dev, access-scope=developer
  - dev-shared: env=dev, access-scope=shared, shared=true
  - staging: env=staging, access-scope=restricted
  - prod: env=prod, access-scope=restricted

2) RBAC (least privilege)
- Per-developer namespaces:
  - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
  - RoleBindings for full control in their own namespace:
    - dev-alice: RoleBinding dev-alice-admin -> ClusterRole admin for subjects: User alice, SA dev-alice/alice-sa
    - dev-bob: RoleBinding dev-bob-admin -> ClusterRole admin for User bob, SA dev-bob/bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: RoleBinding dev-charlie-admin -> ClusterRole admin for User charlie, SA dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Shared namespace (read-only for developers):
  - RoleBinding dev-shared-view-users -> ClusterRole view for Users: alice, bob, charlie
  - RoleBinding dev-shared-view-serviceaccounts -> ClusterRole view for SAs: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging/prod access:
  - No RoleBindings were created for developers; only cluster admins (e.g., users/groups with cluster-admin) can access staging and prod.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - cpu: 2 (requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2)
  - memory: 4Gi (requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi)
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - cpu: 4, memory: 8Gi, pods: 20, services: 10
- staging, prod:
  - cpu: 8, memory: 16Gi, pods: 50, services: 20

4) NetworkPolicies
- Default deny everywhere (except system namespaces): Added default-deny-all (Ingress+Egress) in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod.
- Allow same-namespace traffic: allow-same-namespace (Ingress+Egress) in all six namespaces.
- Allow DNS egress: allow-dns-egress in all six namespaces (to kube-system/kube-dns TCP/UDP 53).
- Allow API server egress (system service): allow-egress-to-apiserver in all six namespaces (to 10.96.0.1:443; uses the clusterIP of the “kubernetes” service).
- Developer-to-shared access only:
  - In dev-* namespaces: allow-egress-to-dev-shared (namespaceSelector by name dev-shared)
  - In dev-shared: allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces (namespaceSelector: env=dev, access-scope=developer)
- Cross-developer isolation:
  - No egress rules from dev-alice to dev-bob/charlie (and vice versa), so those paths remain denied.
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - Only same-namespace traffic, DNS, and API server egress are allowed; no ingress from any dev namespace. This keeps staging/prod completely isolated from dev.

Notes and assumptions
- The “full access” requirement is satisfied with namespace-scoped ClusterRole admin bindings (not cluster-admin). This grants broad control within the namespace (including Secrets/RBAC within the namespace) but no cluster-wide rights.
- System namespaces (kube-system, default, kube-public) were not given default-deny to prevent disrupting cluster components.
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, etc.).
- The developer user identity strings must match your auth provider (“alice”, “bob”, “charlie” here). If your IdP provides different subjects (e.g., emails), adjust the RoleBinding subject names accordingly.

How to validate quickly

RBAC checks
- Own namespace (should be yes):
  - kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' -n dev-alice --as alice
- Read-only in dev-shared (should be yes to get, list; no to create):
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i create pods -n dev-shared --as alice
- No access to other developers’ namespaces (should be no):
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-bob --as alice
- No access to staging/prod (should be no):
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n prod --as alice
- ServiceAccount bindings (example):
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as=system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as=system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa

Network checks (example using temporary pods)
- Allow to dev-shared from dev-alice (should succeed):
  - kubectl -n dev-shared run echo --image=nginxdemos/hello --port=80
  - kubectl -n dev-alice run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- echo.dev-shared.svc.cluster.local
- Block cross-developer (should fail):
  - kubectl -n dev-bob run echo --image=nginxdemos/hello --port=80
  - kubectl -n dev-alice run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- echo.dev-bob.svc.cluster.local
- DNS works (should resolve):
  - kubectl -n dev-alice run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
- Staging/prod isolation (should fail from dev):
  - kubectl -n staging run web --image=nginxdemos/hello --port=80
  - kubectl -n dev-alice run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- web.staging.svc.cluster.local

- Add sensible LimitRanges in each namespace to set default requests/limits aligned to the quotas?

outputSteps.content:
All set. I’ve created the namespaces, RBAC, resource quotas, and network policies to provide a secure, least-privilege, multi-tenant setup for alice, bob, and charlie with strong isolation between dev, staging, and prod.

What I configured

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled for policy selection:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: env=dev, access-scope=developer
  - dev-shared: env=dev, access-scope=shared, shared=true
  - staging: env=staging, access-scope=restricted
  - prod: env=prod, access-scope=restricted

2) RBAC (least privilege)
- Per-developer namespaces:
  - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
  - RoleBindings for full control in their own namespace:
    - dev-alice: RoleBinding dev-alice-admin -> ClusterRole admin for subjects: User alice, SA dev-alice/alice-sa
    - dev-bob: RoleBinding dev-bob-admin -> ClusterRole admin for User bob, SA dev-bob/bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: RoleBinding dev-charlie-admin -> ClusterRole admin for User charlie, SA dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Shared namespace (read-only for developers):
  - RoleBinding dev-shared-view-users -> ClusterRole view for Users: alice, bob, charlie
  - RoleBinding dev-shared-view-serviceaccounts -> ClusterRole view for SAs: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging/prod access:
  - No RoleBindings were created for developers; only cluster admins (e.g., users/groups with cluster-admin) can access staging and prod.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - cpu: 2 (requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2)
  - memory: 4Gi (requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi)
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - cpu: 4, memory: 8Gi, pods: 20, services: 10
- staging, prod:
  - cpu: 8, memory: 16Gi, pods: 50, services: 20

4) NetworkPolicies
- Default deny everywhere (except system namespaces): Added default-deny-all (Ingress+Egress) in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod.
- Allow same-namespace traffic: allow-same-namespace (Ingress+Egress) in all six namespaces.
- Allow DNS egress: allow-dns-egress in all six namespaces (to kube-system/kube-dns TCP/UDP 53).
- Allow API server egress (system service): allow-egress-to-apiserver in all six namespaces (to 10.96.0.1:443; uses the clusterIP of the “kubernetes” service).
- Developer-to-shared access only:
  - In dev-* namespaces: allow-egress-to-dev-shared (namespaceSelector by name dev-shared)
  - In dev-shared: allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces (namespaceSelector: env=dev, access-scope=developer)
- Cross-developer isolation:
  - No egress rules from dev-alice to dev-bob/charlie (and vice versa), so those paths remain denied.
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - Only same-namespace traffic, DNS, and API server egress are allowed; no ingress from any dev namespace. This keeps staging/prod completely isolated from dev.

Notes and assumptions
- The “full access” requirement is satisfied with namespace-scoped ClusterRole admin bindings (not cluster-admin). This grants broad control within the namespace (including Secrets/RBAC within the namespace) but no cluster-wide rights.
- System namespaces (kube-system, default, kube-public) were not given default-deny to prevent disrupting cluster components.
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, etc.).
- The developer user identity strings must match your auth provider (“alice”, “bob”, “charlie” here). If your IdP provides different subjects (e.g., emails), adjust the RoleBinding subject names accordingly.

How to validate quickly

RBAC checks
- Own namespace (should be yes):
  - kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' -n dev-alice --as alice
- Read-only in dev-shared (should be yes to get, list; no to create):
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i create pods -n dev-shared --as alice
- No access to other developers’ namespaces (should be no):
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-bob --as alice
- No access to staging/prod (should be no):
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n prod --as alice
- ServiceAccount bindings (example):
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as=system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as=system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa

Network checks (example using temporary pods)
- Allow to dev-shared from dev-alice (should succeed):
  - kubectl -n dev-shared run echo --image=nginxdemos/hello --port=80
  - kubectl -n dev-alice run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- echo.dev-shared.svc.cluster.local
- Block cross-developer (should fail):
  - kubectl -n dev-bob run echo --image=nginxdemos/hello --port=80
  - kubectl -n dev-alice run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- echo.dev-bob.svc.cluster.local
- DNS works (should resolve):
  - kubectl -n dev-alice run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
